template_name: Hippocampal Pattern Separation and Completion in Environmental Encoding

mechanism_chain.process: Environmental spatial input (configuration of walls, lighting, materials, proportions) enters hippocampus via entorhinal cortex. Input similarity to stored representations is computed along the perforant path to DG.
mechanism_chain.substrate: Entorhinal cortex layer II → DG granule cells

data.finding: Entorhinal cortex provides spatial input to DG via perforant path; similarity computation occurs at this initial stage
data.effect: EC → DG pathway for spatial input

data.finding: DG receives spatial scene input from PPA via EC; input similarity determines whether separation or completion occurs

justification.backing: The EC → DG pathway is the anatomical substrate for similarity computation. Spatial input from scenes and environments enters via this pathway, where the DG determines whether the input is similar enough to stored patterns to trigger completion or different enough to trigger separation.
justification.qualifier: The anatomical pathway is established; the specific computation of architectural feature similarity is inferred from general spatial processing.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if alternative pathways bypass DG for certain spatial inputs; but evidence supports DG as the primary gateway for pattern separation/completion computations.

mechanism_chain.process: If input dissimilarity exceeds separation threshold: DG performs pattern separation — sparse coding via competitive inhibition produces an orthogonal representation in CA3 that does not overlap with stored patterns
mechanism_chain.substrate: DG → mossy fiber → CA3; sparse coding (estimated 2–5% active granule cells)

data.finding: DG granule cells fire sparsely (2-5% active at any time); sparse coding enables pattern separation by reducing overlap between representations
High-resolution fMRI shows DG/CA3 activity distinguishes similar inputs that EC does not distinguish

justification.backing: The DG performs pattern separation through its unique sparse coding architecture. Only 2-5% of granule cells are active at any time, creating highly orthogonal representations even for similar inputs. This is the computational substrate for distinguishing similar spatial environments.
justification.qualifier: The sparse coding mechanism is established; the specific dissimilarity threshold for architectural features is a capacity-derived estimate.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if DG sparse coding is disrupted (as in aging or stress); in these conditions, pattern separation degrades and confusion between similar spaces increases.

mechanism_chain.process: If input similarity exceeds completion threshold: CA3 recurrent collaterals perform pattern completion — partial or degraded input is matched to the closest stored pattern, and the full stored representation is retrieved

data.finding: CA3 recurrent collateral network functions as an auto-associative memory: partial input cues retrieval of full stored pattern
fMRI shows CA3 activity reflects stored pattern even when input is degraded or partial

justification.backing: Marr's theoretical work predicted the CA3 recurrent collateral network would function as an auto-associative memory enabling pattern completion. Empirical evidence from fMRI and electrophysiology confirms this computational role.
justification.qualifier: Pattern completion is established; the boundary between completion and separation is probabilistic and varies with input similarity and individual factors.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if humans rely on different completion mechanisms than predicted by the Marr-McNaughton model; but imaging evidence supports CA3 completion in humans.

mechanism_chain.process: The separation/completion balance determines whether an occupant perceives two adjacent spaces as 'different places' (separation → distinct episodic memories) or 'the same kind of place' (completion → merged or confused memories)
mechanism_chain.substrate: DG-CA3 computational output → downstream CA1 episodic encoding

data.finding: Individuals with better DG pattern separation show less confusion between similar environments and better spatial memory
Aging-related pattern separation decline produces increased confusion between similar spaces
data.source: Yassa et al. (2011); Stark et al. (2013)

justification.backing: The separation/completion balance has direct consequences for wayfinding and spatial memory: too much completion produces confusion between similar corridors; appropriate separation creates distinct memory traces for each space.
justification.qualifier: The behavioral consequence is demonstrated; the specific architectural features that tip the balance are derived from capacity assumptions about feature weighting.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if occupants use non-hippocampal strategies (verbal labels, external landmarks) to distinguish similar spaces; these strategies may compensate for poor pattern separation.

interpersonal_distance.interpretation: Elderly adults require ≥50% feature dissimilarity for reliable pattern separation. Age-related DG dysfunction shifts the threshold upward.
interpersonal_distance.source: Yassa et al. (2011); Stark et al. (2013)

mandatory_distinguishing_dimensions.interpretation: At least one of spatial proportion or lighting must differ between adjacent spaces for separation, regardless of total dissimilarity score. These dimensions are prioritized by hippocampal encoding (PPA pathway).

expertise_familiarity.interpretation: Minimum 5 of 8 feature dimensions must differ between adjacent spaces (elderly adults)

age_group.effect: Separation threshold increases by ~0.15 (from 0.35 to 0.50); pattern completion bias increases; DG neurogenesis decline is primary mechanism
age_group.mechanism: Reduced DG granule cell neurogenesis; perforant path degradation (Small et al., 2011; Yassa et al., 2011)

clinical_condition.effect: Chronic cortisol exposure impairs DG neurogenesis and pattern separation; similar direction to aging but via glucocorticoid mechanism

IC2_AX4_interaction.IC2_body_budget: Allostatic load degrades pattern separation capacity via cortisol-mediated DG suppression. In hospital and eldercare contexts, occupants in allostatic deficit have BOTH age-related and stress-related impairment of pattern separation — a compounding vulnerability that demands more distinctive spatial design.
IC2_AX4_interaction.AX4_perceived_control: Low perceived control increases reliance on pattern completion (familiar = safe heuristic). Occupants with low control perception in an unfamiliar building default to completion, which means they are more likely to confuse similar spaces and become disoriented.

cross_template_references: ED_HIPPOCAMPAL_ENCODING_001 — shares feature dimension weights and distinctiveness threshold
STRESS-I T6 — cortisol impairs DG-mediated pattern separation
THRESHOLD_EPISODIC_BOUNDARY_001 — thresholds that trigger pattern separation also trigger episodic boundaries

spatial_configuration.interpretation: Computed using feature dimension weights from ED_HIPPOCAMPAL_ENCODING_001; corridors scoring below threshold are predicted to produce wayfinding confusion

landmark_density.interpretation: Distinctive landmarks at decision points (intersections, turns) provide additional separation cues beyond ambient spatial features
